title: Sequences and Summations
references: Kenneth H. Rosen, Discrete Mathematics and Its Applications, eighth edition, §2.4.1–§2.4.5, printed pages 165–177 (exposition), with a labeled telescoping-sum extension.
Original companion explanations, examples, diagrams, and practice checks.

units.title: 1. Treat the position as the input of a function

blocks.text: A sequence assigns a value to each allowed integer position. The position matters, and repeated values are allowed. A summation then adds selected terms; it is a different object from the sequence itself.

In aₙ, n is the index and aₙ is the term at that index. A sequence is a function from an integer index set to a set of values. We write (aₙ) here; the textbook also uses {aₙ}, which denotes a sequence in that context, not an unordered set.

For aₙ = 2n + 3 with n = 0, 1, 2, …, the first terms are 3, 5, 7, 9, …. The first term is a₀ = 3, while a₁ = 5 is the second term. If the domain instead starts at 1, the first term is 5: the formula alone does not tell you where to begin.

rows: Three positions; the first two have equal values.
Two distinct members; no first or second member.
One number, obtained by adding all three terms.

blocks.prompt: If aₙ = 1/(n + 1) for n ≥ 0, what are a₀ and a₃?

explanation.text: a₀ = 1 and a₃ = 1/4. Substitute the index, not the position’s informal name. This indexing avoids dividing by zero.

blocks.text: Textbook connection: §2.4.1–§2.4.2, printed page 165.

units.title: 2. Ask whether each step adds or multiplies

blocks.text: With indexing from 1, write aₙ = a₁ + (n − 1)d or aₙ = a₁rⁿ⁻¹. The exponent or coefficient counts the number of steps from the initial index. A negative ratio alternates signs; a ratio between 0 and 1 shrinks a positive initial value.

For r = 0, define the geometric sequence by its initial term and repeated multiplication: a₀, 0, 0, …. This avoids an unexplained 0⁰ at index zero. Dividing successive terms to find a ratio is useful only when the denominator is nonzero.

blocks.prompt: The first term is b₁ = 7 and the common difference is 4. Find b₅.

explanation.text: b₅ = 7 + (5 − 1)·4 = 23. There are four steps between positions 1 and 5, not five.

blocks.text: Textbook connection: §2.4.2, printed page 166.

units.title: 3. Keep repetitions and the empty string

blocks.text: A finite sequence of symbols is a string. Its length is its number of positions. For example, abba has length 4 even though only two distinct symbols occur. Concatenation places one string after another: ab followed by ba gives abba.

The empty string has length zero. The textbook denotes it by λ; ε is another common convention. It differs from the empty set and from a string containing one blank space. Appending the empty string changes nothing.

blocks.prompt: Compare the lengths of 0101, 0, and the empty string. How many distinct symbols occur in 0101?

explanation.text: The lengths are 4, 1, and 0. The string 0101 uses two distinct symbols, 0 and 1, but length counts occurrences and positions, not distinct symbols.

blocks.text: Textbook connection: §2.4.2, printed page 166.

units.title: 4. Supply initial values before applying a recurrence

blocks.text: A recurrence expresses a term using earlier terms. Initial conditions supply the values needed before that rule starts. State the first index where the rule is valid.

blocks.notation: a₀ = 4; aₙ = aₙ₋₁ + 5 for integers n ≥ 1
blocks.description: This determines one new term from its predecessor.

blocks.title: Two previous values need two starting values

blocks.text: For b₀ = 2, b₁ = 5, and bₙ = bₙ₋₁ − bₙ₋₂ for n ≥ 2, we get b₂ = 3, b₃ = −2, b₄ = −5, and b₅ = −3. Omitting b₁ would leave the later terms undetermined.

For a rule that assigns exactly one next value from already determined earlier values, enough initial conditions determine a unique sequence. An equation with multiple possible next values needs additional choices; “recurrence” alone does not guarantee uniqueness.

blocks.prompt: Does aₙ = aₙ₋₁ + 5 by itself determine a₃?

explanation.text: No. Starting at a₀ = 4 gives a₃ = 19; starting at a₀ = 0 gives a₃ = 15. The rule describes how to move, while the initial value fixes where you start.

blocks.text: Textbook connection: §2.4.3, printed pages 167–168.

units.title: 5. Compare familiar sequences by their rules and initial values

blocks.notation: F₀ = 0, F₁ = 1; Fₙ = Fₙ₋₁ + Fₙ₋₂ for n ≥ 2
blocks.description: Each Fibonacci term after the first two is the sum of its two predecessors.

blocks.text: The second row uses the same addition rule but initial values L₀ = 2 and L₁ = 1. It is the Lucas sequence under indexing from zero. Shared recurrence does not mean shared sequence.

blocks.notation: c₀ = 1; cₙ = n cₙ₋₁ for n ≥ 1, so cₙ = n!
blocks.description: Factorials multiply by the current index; the multiplier is not a fixed geometric ratio.

blocks.prompt: Compute F₈ and L₈, and explain why their values differ.

explanation.text: F₈ = 13 + 8 = 21, while L₈ = 29 + 18 = 47. The same recurrence has carried their different starting values forward.

blocks.text: Textbook connection: §2.4.3, printed pages 167–168; §2.4.4, printed page 171.

units.title: 6. Check the rule and the initial conditions separately

blocks.text: A sequence may satisfy a recurrence but fail the specified initial conditions. Solving an initial-value problem requires both checks.

blocks.notation: aₙ = 2aₙ₋₁ − aₙ₋₂ for n ≥ 2; a₀ = 2, a₁ = 5
blocks.description: We will test candidates against the recurrence and against both starting values.

blocks.title: Verify the successful candidate for every index

blocks.text: For n ≥ 2, substitute aₙ₋₁ = 3(n − 1) + 2 and aₙ₋₂ = 3(n − 2) + 2. Then 2[3(n − 1) + 2] − [3(n − 2) + 2] = 3n + 2 = aₙ. The separate checks at n = 0 and n = 1 give 2 and 5. Thus the formula meets every requirement.

blocks.prompt: Why is checking only n = 2, 3, and 4 not a proof for all n?

explanation.text: A finite sample can expose errors but cannot cover infinitely many indices. The algebraic substitution above uses an arbitrary n ≥ 2, so it checks the recurrence generally.

blocks.text: Textbook connection: §2.4.3, printed page 168.

units.title: 7. Count substitutions back to the actual starting index

blocks.text: Iteration repeatedly substitutes a recurrence to reveal a closed formula: one that gives a term directly from its index without computing all predecessors. Continue the rule a₀ = 4, aₙ = aₙ₋₁ + 5.

Forward calculation gives 4, 9, 14, 19, … and suggests the same rule. To certify it, the base n = 0 gives 4. If aₙ₋₁ = 4 + 5(n − 1), then the recurrence gives aₙ = 4 + 5(n − 1) + 5 = 4 + 5n. This is the induction pattern from Chapter 5.

blocks.prompt: What if the statement instead says a₁ = 4 and the recurrence starts at n = 2?

explanation.text: Then there are n − 1 steps from a₁ to aₙ, so aₙ = 4 + 5(n − 1). Test the initial index: putting n = 1 must return 4. Do not switch between a₀ and a₁ midway through a derivation.

blocks.text: Textbook connection: §2.4.3, printed pages 168–169.

units.title: 8. Translate a repeated percentage change into multiplication

blocks.text: Suppose a modeled quantity starts at P₀ = 80 units and increases by 25% of its current value each period, with no additions, losses, or rounding. Then Pₙ = Pₙ₋₁ + 0.25Pₙ₋₁ = 1.25Pₙ₋₁. Iteration gives Pₙ = 80(1.25)ⁿ.

The percentage applies to the changing current quantity. Adding a fixed 20 units each period would describe a different, arithmetic model. Fractional values here are allowed model quantities, not counts of indivisible objects. A real process with per-period rounding or varying rates needs a different recurrence.

blocks.prompt: If the model instead loses 25% each period, is the multiplier −0.25?

explanation.text: No. It retains 75%, so the multiplier is 0.75 and Pₙ = 80(0.75)ⁿ. A negative multiplier would alternate signs.

blocks.text: Textbook connection: §2.4.3, printed page 169.

units.title: 9. Treat an observed pattern as a candidate rule

blocks.text: Look for constant differences, constant ratios, repeated blocks, cycles, or combinations of previous terms. These can suggest a rule, but finitely many terms do not determine an infinite sequence uniquely.

blocks.title: Two rules can fit the same data

blocks.text: For n ≥ 1, both aₙ = 3n + 1 and bₙ = 3n + 1 + (n − 1)(n − 2)(n − 3)(n − 4) begin 4, 7, 10, 13. The added product is zero at those four indices. At n = 5, a₅ = 16 but b₅ = 40. The observations alone cannot choose between them.

A sequence database such as the OEIS, discussed in the textbook, can suggest matches. A match is evidence for a conjecture, not a proof that its rule describes your problem. Check the indexing, definition, and a derivation from the original problem.

blocks.prompt: If the differences of the first six terms are all 3, can you conclude every later difference is 3?

explanation.text: Only if the sequence is defined by a rule or argument that guarantees it. A finite list by itself supports a plausible conjecture, not a unique continuation.

blocks.text: Textbook connection: §2.4.4, printed pages 170–172.

units.title: 10. Build a small library without losing the starting index

blocks.text: The list 3, 6, 11, 18, 27 is two more than 1², 2², 3², 4², 5². A candidate is aₙ = n² + 2 for n ≥ 1. Its successive differences are 3, 5, 7, 9, which also suggest a quadratic pattern. This is still a candidate unless the problem supplies more structure.

blocks.prompt: Why is F₁, F₂, F₃, … different from the full list starting at F₀?

explanation.text: The first list starts 1, 1, 2, …; the second starts 0, 1, 1, 2, …. They use the same Fibonacci rule, but the displayed index range differs. Record that range when comparing lists.

blocks.text: Textbook connection: §2.4.4, printed pages 170–172.

units.title: 11. Expand a summation before simplifying it

blocks.description: Read “sum a sub j from j = m through n.” The bounds are inclusive integers; for m ≤ n there are n − m + 1 terms.

blocks.text: The expression being added is the summand, and j is a bound or dummy index. Renaming j to k everywhere inside the same sum changes nothing. The upper bound n may remain a free parameter.

A sum over an empty index set is 0. In the finite integer-range convention used here, a lower bound larger than the upper bound means no terms. A zero-term sum differs from a sum with one term equal to zero, even though their values agree.

blocks.prompt: How many terms are in Σⱼ₌₀ⁿ aⱼ for n ≥ 0? What if n = 0?

explanation.text: There are n + 1 terms. At n = 0 the sum is a₀, not an empty sum. Count both endpoints.

blocks.text: Textbook connection: §2.4.5, printed pages 172–173.

units.title: 12. Split addition, but do not split a product into separate sums

blocks.notation: Σⱼ₌ₘⁿ (c aⱼ + d bⱼ) = c Σⱼ₌ₘⁿ aⱼ + d Σⱼ₌ₘⁿ bⱼ
blocks.description: For finite sums, c and d are constants with respect to the summation index.

blocks.text: Σⱼ₌₁⁴ (3j + 2) = 3(1 + 2 + 3 + 4) + 2·4 = 30 + 8 = 38. The constant 2 appears four times. It is not added just once.
For a₁ = 1, a₂ = 2 and b₁ = 3, b₂ = 4, we have Σⱼ₌₁² aⱼbⱼ = 1·3 + 2·4 = 11. But (Σⱼ₌₁² aⱼ)(Σⱼ₌₁² bⱼ) = 3·7 = 21. The product of sums includes cross terms with different indices.

blocks.prompt: Can you pull j outside Σⱼ₌₁⁴ j aⱼ?

explanation.text: No. It changes as the index changes. You can pull out a quantity only when it is constant with respect to that sum’s index. In an inner sum over j, an outer index i may be temporarily constant.

blocks.text: Textbook connection: §2.4.5, printed page 173.

units.title: 13. Change the index, bounds, and summand together

blocks.text: To reindex Σⱼ₌₃⁶ j² starting at zero, define k = j − 3. Then j = k + 3. Translate the lower endpoint 3 to 0, the upper endpoint 6 to 3, and every j in the summand to k + 3.

blocks.description: The labels change; the four terms being added stay the same.

blocks.title: Match each old index to one new index
blocks.description: Four aligned columns show old indices 3,4,5,6 above new indices 0,1,2,3. The corresponding squared terms remain 9,16,25,36.

blocks.prompt: Why is Σₖ₌₀³ k² not the reindexed version?

explanation.text: It adds 0 + 1 + 4 + 9 = 14, a different list. Changing only the bounds loses the shift inside the summand. Verify the first and last terms after every reindexing.

blocks.text: Textbook connection: §2.4.5, printed pages 173–174.

units.title: 14. Derive a geometric sum by canceling the shared terms

blocks.text: For a real first term a, nonzero ratio r, and integer n ≥ 0, let S = a + ar + … + arⁿ. There are n + 1 terms. Multiply by r, then subtract the original sum.

blocks.notation:
Σⱼ₌₀ⁿ arʲ = a(rⁿ⁺¹ − 1)/(r − 1), if r ≠ 1
Σⱼ₌₀ⁿ a = (n + 1)a, if r = 1
blocks.description: For r ≠ 1 divide (r − 1)S = a(rⁿ⁺¹ − 1) by the nonzero r − 1. The r = 1 case must be handled separately.

blocks.text: For a = 2, r = 3, and n = 4, the terms are 2, 6, 18, 54, 162. Their sum is 242. The formula gives 2(3⁵ − 1)/(3 − 1) = 242. The exponent 5 reflects five terms.
For r = 0, use the recurrence interpretation a, 0, 0, … from the progression unit; every nonempty initial sum is a. This treats the initial value explicitly rather than silently using 0⁰.

explanation.text: Here a = 5, r = 1, and n = 3. Use the special case (3 + 1)·5 = 20. Substituting r = 1 into the quotient would divide by zero.

blocks.text: Textbook connection: §2.4.5, printed page 174, Theorem 1.

units.title: 15. Use prefix sums to handle arbitrary starting points

blocks.text: At n = 0 these are empty sums and all three formulas give zero. The first formula follows by pairing the first and last terms: adding the sum to its reverse gives n copies of n + 1. The formulas can also be verified by induction: the value at n minus the value at n − 1 must equal the new summand, with a matching base case.

blocks.title: Subtract the prefix before the requested interval

blocks.text: To find Σₖ₌₄⁸ k², take the sum through 8 and remove the sum through 3. The result is 8·9·17/6 − 3·4·7/6 = 204 − 14 = 190. Removing through 4 would remove a term we still need.

blocks.notation: Σₖ₌ₘⁿ aₖ = S(n) − S(m − 1), where S(t) = Σₖ₌₁ᵗ aₖ and 1 ≤ m ≤ n
blocks.description: The prefix ends immediately before the first desired index.

blocks.text: For N terms a₀, a₀ + d, …, a₀ + (N − 1)d, the sum is Na₀ + dN(N − 1)/2. For 8, 5, 2, −1, take N = 4 and d = −3: 4·8 − 3·4·3/2 = 14.

explanation.text: Use linearity: the square sum is 30 and twice the integer sum is 20, giving 50. Direct expansion gives 3 + 8 + 15 + 24 = 50.

blocks.text: Textbook connection: §2.4.5, printed pages 175–176, Table 2.

units.title: 16. Hold the outer index fixed while doing the inner sum

blocks.description: For each i, first add the four values obtained by varying j. Then add the three row totals.

blocks.text: The total is 14 + 18 + 22 = 54. Summing columns instead gives 9 + 12 + 15 + 18 = 54. Reordering a finite sum over the same pairs does not change it.

blocks.title: Bounds can depend on the outer index

blocks.text: For Σᵢ₌₁⁴ Σⱼ₌₁ⁱ 1, row i has i terms. The total is 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10. If you reverse the order, the same pairs satisfy 1 ≤ j ≤ 4 and j ≤ i ≤ 4, giving Σⱼ₌₁⁴ Σᵢ₌ⱼ⁴ 1. Simply swapping index letters while keeping incompatible bounds would count a different region.

blocks.title: A set can be the index collection

blocks.text: Σₛ∈{−2,1,3} s² = (−2)² + 1² + 3² = 14. Sum once for each member of the index set. Repeating a member in its written roster does not add another index.

blocks.prompt: In Σᵢ₌₁³ Σⱼ₌₁⁴ i, how many times is each i added?

explanation.text: Four times in its inner sum. The result is Σᵢ₌₁³ 4i = 4(1 + 2 + 3) = 24. The inner index j does not appear in the summand, but its range still determines the repetition count.

blocks.text: Textbook connection: §2.4.5, printed page 175.

units.title: 17. Look for cancellation before expanding everything

blocks.text: A telescoping sum has neighboring terms that cancel. This is a useful extension of finite summation rules; write the first few and last terms so the surviving endpoints are visible.
Every internal fraction appears once with each sign. Only the first positive and last negative terms survive. Since 1/k − 1/(k + 1) = 1/[k(k + 1)], the same formula evaluates Σₖ₌₁ⁿ 1/[k(k + 1)].

explanation.text: The surviving terms are 1/3 − 1/7 = 4/21. Starting at 3 changes the first surviving endpoint; do not automatically start the answer at 1.

blocks.text: Textbook connection: §2.4.5, printed pages 172–176; companion extension.

units.title: 18. Keep infinite series separate from long finite sums

blocks.text: An infinite series is defined through the limit of its finite partial sums, when that limit exists. It is not a finite sum with a very large upper bound. The following two formulas require |x| < 1.

blocks.notation:
Σₖ₌₀∞ xᵏ = 1/(1 − x), for |x| < 1
Σₖ₌₁∞ kxᵏ⁻¹ = 1/(1 − x)², for |x| < 1
blocks.description: In the second formula the first term is 1, including at x = 0; it is the constant term.

blocks.text: For the first formula, the finite sum through N equals (1 − xᴺ⁺¹)/(1 − x). When |x| < 1, xᴺ⁺¹ tends to zero, so the partial sums tend to 1/(1 − x). The remaining tail after index N is xᴺ⁺¹/(1 − x). At x = 1, partial sums grow without bound; at x = −1 they alternate between 1 and 0 and have no limit.

The second formula follows by differentiating the geometric power series inside |x| < 1. A calculus theorem justifies differentiating term by term there; that step is not valid for arbitrary infinite sums. At x = 1/2, the two sums are 2 and 4, respectively.

explanation.text: No. This finite sum has six terms and equals 2 − 1/32 = 63/32. The infinite sum equals 2; its tail after index 5 is 1/32.

blocks.text: State the index range and starting values. Distinguish a term, a sequence, and a sum. Check a recurrence at its initial indices before proving the general rule. When summing, count the terms, preserve both endpoints during reindexing, and verify every formula’s conditions.
Section 2.5 uses functions to compare the sizes of sets, including infinite sets. Section 2.6 introduces matrices. Those are the next numbered sections in this chapter.
Textbook connection: §2.4.5, printed pages 176–177; review of §2.4.
